---
title: "Examples"
subtitle: "Grids laid out by the extension."
description: "Working Masonry grids built by the extension, with the attributes behind each and the JSON they produce."
---

::: {.callout-caution}
This extension is experimental, and its interface may still change.
:::

Every grid below is laid out by Masonry as this page loads.
Resize the window and they reflow.

The site sets its defaults in `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
extensions:
  masonry:
    item-selector: ".grid-item"
    gutter: 10
    percent-position: true
```

The items are sized by this site's own stylesheet, since the extension styles nothing.
The [Reference](reference.qmd#attributes) lists every attribute, and [Precedence](reference.qmd#precedence) says which value wins.

## A grid

```markdown
:::: {.grid}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--width2}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--width2}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::

:::

The items are of uneven height, and Masonry packs them rather than leaving the gaps a float layout would.

## Changing the gutter

`masonry-gutter` overrides the document default for one grid.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-gutter="30"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-gutter="30"}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::::

:::

## Setting the column width

`masonry-column-width` sets the width of one column.
A grid without the attribute has no column width, so Masonry measures the first item and uses that width instead.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-column-width="200"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-column-width="200"}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--width2}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::

:::

Each item here is 150 pixels wide and the column is 200 pixels.
Masonry adds the gutter to the column, so the items sit 210 pixels apart and a gap opens beside each one.

A value that is not a number is read as a CSS selector.
Masonry looks for that selector inside the grid and measures the width of the first element it finds.
A selector that matches nothing breaks the layout, because Masonry then uses the selector text itself as the width.

## Keeping horizontal order

`masonry-horizontal-order="true"` keeps items in left-to-right order rather than packing them as tightly as possible.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-horizontal-order="true"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-horizontal-order="true"}
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::

:::

## Choosing which children to lay out

`masonry-item-selector` names the children Masonry lays out.
The grid below gives every child a `.demo-card` class and lays out that class rather than the default `.grid-item`.
The children keep `.grid-item` as well, because this site's stylesheet sizes them by that class.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-item-selector=".demo-card"}
::: {.grid-item .demo-card}
:::
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-item-selector=".demo-card"}
::: {.grid-item .demo-card}
:::
::: {.grid-item .demo-card .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item .demo-card}
:::
::: {.grid-item .demo-card .grid-item--height3}
:::
::::

:::

Masonry lays out each child that matches the selector, and leaves every other child where the browser put it.
A selector that matches nothing therefore lays out nothing.

## Positioning in percentages

`masonry-percent-position` decides the unit Masonry writes an item's horizontal position in.
This site turns it on for every grid, and one grid turns it off again below.
The attribute is how a document default is overridden for a single grid.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-percent-position="false"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-percent-position="false"}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::::

:::

The grid produces `{ "gutter": 10, "itemSelector": ".grid-item", "percentPosition": false }`.
The packing is the same as the other grids, and the inline styles are not.
Masonry writes the horizontal position of an item in pixels here, and as a percentage of the grid width everywhere else on this page.
Inspect an item in your browser to see which unit it carries.

## Animating the reflow

`masonry-transition-duration` sets how long an item takes to move to a new position.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-transition-duration="1s"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-transition-duration="1s"}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--width2}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::

:::

The first layout is instant, so nothing animates while the page loads.
Masonry animates every later layout, and a window resize that changes the width of the grid starts one.
Make the window narrower against the grid above, and the items take a full second to glide to their new columns.

Always give this value a unit.
The extension sends the option to Masonry as a string, so a bare `200` reaches the CSS `transition-duration` property as `200`, which is not a valid CSS time.
Write `200ms` or `0.2s` instead.
`0s` turns the animation off, and the items jump straight to their new positions.

## Staggering the reflow

`masonry-stagger` delays each item behind the one before it.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-stagger="150" masonry-transition-duration="1s"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid masonry-stagger="150" masonry-transition-duration="1s"}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--width2}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height3}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::

:::

Resize the window against the grid above.
The first item moves at once, the second 150 milliseconds later, the third 300 milliseconds later, and so on down the grid.
Compare it with the grid in the section before, where every item moves together.

A bare number is read as milliseconds.
A string with a unit is read as a CSS time, so `150`, `150ms` and `0.15s` all give the same delay.

## Raw JSON still wins

A key written in `data-masonry` is never overwritten; the friendly attributes fill in only what it leaves out.

```markdown
:::: {.grid data-masonry='{ "gutter": 0 }' masonry-gutter="40"}
::::
```

::: {.masonry-demo}

:::: {.grid data-masonry='{ "gutter": 0 }' masonry-gutter="40"}
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::: {.grid-item .grid-item--height2}
:::
::: {.grid-item}
:::
::::

:::

The gutter is `0`, from the JSON, not `40` from the attribute.
The document defaults still merge in around it, so the grid ends up with `{ "gutter": 0, "itemSelector": ".grid-item", "percentPosition": true }`.

## Waiting for images

A grid of images lays out before the images have dimensions, then jumps once they arrive.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-wait-for-images="true" masonry-wait-for-images-timeout="3000"}
::: {.grid-item}
![](image-1.jpg)
:::
::::
```

The timeout caps the wait, so a request that never resolves delays the layout rather than cancelling it.

## A value the extension reports

`column-width`, `gutter` and `stagger` reach Masonry exactly as written, and a negative number is reported while the document renders.

```markdown
:::: {.grid masonry-gutter="-10"}
::::
```

That grid is not rendered on this page, because its warning would appear in this site's own build.
The render prints one line:

```text
(W) [masonry] Option 'gutter' is negative (-10); Masonry.js expects a non-negative value.
```

The grid still gets `{ "gutter": -10, "itemSelector": ".grid-item", "percentPosition": true }`, so the output shows what you supplied rather than a silent substitution.
See [Invalid values](reference.qmd#invalid-values) for the values the extension drops instead.
